Osteochondral Lesions of the Talus
 CORE

FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review the pathophysiology, etiology, and classification of osteochondral lesions of the talus.
Determine appropriate evaluation and workup for a patient with an osteochondral lesion of
the talus.
Describe nonsurgical and surgical treatment options and outcomes based on lesion
characteristics.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Osteochondral lesions of the talus (OLTs) are injuries to the talar cartilage surface and the
underlying subchondral bone.




NOTES

May result from acute trauma, such as ankle sprains and ankle fractures, or repetitive
microtrauma or may be atraumatic
Epidemiology
Relatively common in patients with ankle trauma, observed in as many as 73% of ankle
fractures
4% of osteochondral injuries
Natural history unclear; however, asymptomatic and minimally symptomatic lesions can be
managed nonsurgically, with low rates of progression

Epidemiology
OLTs are relatively common injuries observed in patients with or without trauma. The
term OLT incorporates several historically used phrases, including osteochondritis
dissecans, osteochondral fracture, and osteochondral injury. A study of active-duty US
military members demonstrated that OLTs may be more common than initially thought,
with 27 per 100,000 patient-years in a 10-year period noted in this patient population.1
OLTs are observed in as many as 73% of patients with an ankle fracture;2 however, a
broad range is reported in the literature. Cartilage injury is thought to occur in
approximately 50% of patients with an acute ankle sprain.3 The prevalence approaches
70% in patients with chronic ankle instability and may be higher in patients with deltoid
instability.4 Bilateral lesions are more common in the medial aspect of the talus and
have been reported to occur in 10% of individuals.5
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The talus has no muscular attachments. Cartilage covers more than 60% of its surface.
Most osteochondral lesions occur in the medial and lateral aspects of the talar dome.
Medial lesions are more common and tend to be deeper.
Lateral lesions tend to be shallower and are more likely displaced.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:28 PM
AAOS | Osteochondral Lesions of the Talus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000007
2/28

Lesions are most commonly centromedial and centrolateral in the dome.
Vascular
Vascular supply to the talus is tenuous and may be related to the reason these lesions are
prone to occur.

Vascular
The talus is a complex bone, with most of the surface covered with cartilage. The
posterior aspect of the bone is narrower than the anterior aspect of the bone. Using a
nine-section grid to evaluate lesion location, several authors have reported that most
OLTs are located at the centromedial and centrolateral dome.6,7 Traditionally, lesions
were more commonly thought to be anteromedial and posterolateral. Lateral lesions
often are more traumatic, symptomatic, and surgically managed.8 OLTs are prone to
occur for several reasons and are difficult entities to manage. The retrograde blood
supply to the talar body is tenuous, potentially impairing healing of these lesions. The
talar cartilage is thinner than that of the knee and hip, adding to the propensity of these
lesions to occur. Depending on the size and location of the lesion, the medial malleolus
and fibula may impede ideal access, further adding to the challenge of appropriately
managing OLTs.
Etiology
May be atraumatic; more commonly result from acute trauma, such as ankle sprains and ankle
fractures, or repetitive microtrauma
Atraumatic lesions are thought to be a disruption of the subchondral bone that affects the
overlying cartilage, likely because of ischemia.
Medial lesions are commonly atraumatic and tend to be larger.
Bilateral in 10% of patients with no history of trauma
Lateral lesions more often are associated with a traumatic etiology and tend to be smaller but
are associated with a greater likelihood of displacement than medial lesions.


Etiology
Although OLTs may be atraumatic, most result from a traumatic event or repetitive
microtrauma. An atraumatic OLT likely is the result of disruption of the subchondral
bone that negatively affects the health of the overlying cartilage, likely related to
ischemia. Atraumatic lesions often are more in a medial location and are larger and
deeper than lateral lesions. The mechanism of traumatic subchondral injury of the
lateral talar dome is axial load combined with inversion in a dorsiflexed position,
whereas axial load combined with inversion, plantarflexion, and external rotation results
in impaction medially.9
Natural History
Natural history of OLTs is variable
OLTs do not predictably progress to arthritis.

Natural History
The natural history of nonsurgically managed lesions is a subject of debate because
many patients with a symptomatic lesion are treated surgically. A small short-term study
evaluating the MRIs of 29 patients who were treated nonsurgically reported that 45% of
the OLTs progressed in size, 24% of the OLTs improved, and 31% of the OLTs
demonstrated no clear change during a 14-month period.10 Two more recent, longer
term retrospective studies of patients treated nonsurgically during a mean period of 4
and 6 years reported good clinical outcomes and low prevalence of lesion progression
(zero and 11%).11,12 End-stage arthritis is not common.
Risk Factors
Trauma: ankle and hindfoot fracture, ankle sprain
Ankle instability

Classification


Classification
Classification systems for OLTs evolved from systems based on radiographic findings to
systems based on CT and MRI findings. The classification systems are descriptive but do
not have much effect on management because they do not account for lesion size.
The first classification system, published in 1959 by Berndt and Harty, was based on the
degree of osteochondral fragment detachment observed on radiographs.9 Stage 1 is a
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:28 PM
AAOS | Osteochondral Lesions of the Talus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000007
7/28

subchondral compression injury, stage 2 is an osteochondral fragment that is partially
detached, stage 3 is detached but not displaced, and stage 4 is displaced. This
classification system has not correlated particularly well with arthroscopic findings.
The Ferkel and Sgaglione CT classification system was created in 1990 and better
correlates with arthroscopic findings.13 Stage 1 is an underlying cystic lesion with intact
bony rim, stage 2a is a cystic lesion with communication to the surface, stage 2b is an
open lesion with an overlying fragment, stage 3 is a nondisplaced lesion with underlying
lucency, and stage 4 is a displaced fragment.
In 1999 the Hepple et al14 proposed a MRI classification system, with stage 1 injury
isolated to the articular cartilage; stage 2a, cartilage injury with bone injury and edema;
stage 2b, without surrounding edema; stage 3, detached but nondisplaced lesion; stage
4, displaced bony lesion; and stage 5, with subchondral cyst.
The arthroscopic classification system is based on intraoperative findings: stage A,
smooth and intact but soft; stage B, rough articular surface; stage C, fibrillations/fissures;
stage D, flap present or bone exposed; stage E, loose, nondisplaced fragment; and stage
F, displaced fragment15 (Resource 1).
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Possible history of trauma
Symptoms include swelling, pain, instability, catching, or locking

Patient History
In most patients, a diagnosis of OLT is not made on initial examination but is identified
on radiographs or advanced imaging studies. Typical symptoms include pain with weight
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:28 PM
AAOS | Osteochondral Lesions of the Talus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000007
8/28

bearing, ankle joint effusion, mechanical symptoms, and instability. The patient may
describe an acute traumatic event, may note chronic instability, or may have symptoms
without a definite injury.
Physical Examination
Effusion
Ankle instability
Joint line tenderness
Hindfoot alignment

Physical Examination
Physical examination of a patient in whom an OLT is suspected may reveal tibiotalar joint
effusion and painful or limited range of motion. Joint line tenderness may be present,
and ankle instability may be noted. Alternatively, the patient may describe pain with
weight bearing and activity, but tenderness may not be reproducible. Examining
hindfoot alignment is critical to diagnose concomitant hindfoot varus that may
contribute to ankle instability.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiographs may appear normal or demonstrate subtle radiolucency, cystic changes, or bone
fragmentation. Less commonly they may reveal a displaced fragment.

Radiography
Weight-bearing AP, mortise, and lateral radiographs of the ankle are routinely obtained.
The talar dome may appear normal if the injury is isolated to the cartilage or bony
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:28 PM

9/28

involvement is subtle. Radiographs may demonstrate fragmentation of the subchondral
bone, cystic changes deep to the subchondral bone, or a displaced osteochondral
fragment (Figure 2).
Figure 2 Mortise radiograph of an ankle shows a subchondral lucency in the lateral talar
dome (arrow). (Reproduced from Frey C: Osteochondral lesions of the talus, in Johnson
RT, Steinbach LS, eds: Essentials of Musculoskeletal Imaging. Rosemont, IL, Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2004, pp 616-619.)
Computed Tomography
A CT scan often is obtained if an OLT with bony involvement or cystic changes is observed on
radiographs or MRIs.
Weight-bearing CT may be considered in patients with concomitant deformity.

Computed Tomography

picture of cystic change, bone voids, overall lesion size, and size and location of a
displaced bony fragment16 (Figure 3).
Figure 3 Coronal CT scan of an ankle shows a lateral talar dome osteochondral lesion.

Chou LB, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Foot and Ankle, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2014, pp 387-399.)
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Routinely performed in patients with an OLT to assess the cartilage surface and surrounding
soft tissues (Figure 4).
The most sensitive imaging modality to detect an OLT
MRI may overestimate the size of a lesion because of surrounding edema but is more sensitive
with regard to the diagnosis of cartilage damage on the talar and tibial surfaces and also
allows for assessment of the surrounding ligaments and tendons. MRI is more sensitive than
CT at detecting lesions and correlates well with arthroscopic findings.17
Figure 4 Coronal (A) and sagittal (B) T2-weighted MRIs of a left ankle show a lateral talar dome
osteochondral lesion. (Reproduced from Chao W, Freeland E, Dedini R: Osteochondral lesions of
the talus, in Chou LB, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Foot and Ankle, ed 5. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2014, pp 387-399.)
Diagnosis
Diagnosis is made via imaging studies.
SEND FEEDBACK

AAOS | Osteochondral Lesions of the Talus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000007
12/28


Diagnosis
In a patient in whom an OLT is suspected, radiographs should be obtained and reviewed.
Advanced imaging studies usually are performed, with MRI performed routinely and CT
performed if assessment of the bony architecture is necessary, such as in a patient with
a cystic lesion or to assess the continuity of subchondral bone. Occasionally, an OLT is
diagnosed intraoperatively, either via arthroscopy or via direct visualization of the joint
surface, during another procedure, such as fracture fixation.
Differential Diagnosis
Ankle impingement
Tibiotalar arthritis
Tibial osteochondral lesion
Tibiotalar synovitis
Occult fracture
Tarsal coalition
Posterior impingement
Instability: lateral, medial, and/or syndesmotic

Differential Diagnosis
The differential diagnosis for OLTs is broad and should be considered in patients with
chronic or posttraumatic ankle pain. The diagnosis is confirmed on imaging studies.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Asymptomatic patient
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:28 PM
AAOS | Osteochondral Lesions of the Talus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000007
13/28

Nondisplaced lesion

Indications
A trial of nonsurgical management is appropriate in patients with a nondisplaced or
minimally displaced lesion. Asymptomatic lesions found incidentally also can be
managed nonsurgically. Patients with symptomatic lesions can undergo a trial of
immobilization followed by physical therapy. Approximately 3 to 6 months of nonsurgical
management is attempted. No clear optimal nonsurgical treatment protocol exists. In
general, immobilization in a boot or brace, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications,
activity modifications, and physical therapy are used.18
Relative Contraindications
Acute displaced osteochondral fragment

Relative Contraindications
An acute displaced osteochondral fracture generally is managed surgically. If the bony
fragment is large enough, the fragment can be fixed primarily via buried metal or
absorbable fixation.19 If the bony rim is too small for fixation, if it is an isolated cartilage
fragment, or if the piece is not salvageable, then the fragment can be excised, and the
bony bed managed based on the size of the defect.
Surgical Management
Based on lesion size and location

Surgical Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:28 PM
AAOS | Osteochondral Lesions of the Talus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000007
14/28

If surgical management is selected, several techniques that are traditionally based on
lesion size, depth, location, and chronicity are available. Surgical treatment options
include débridement alone, marrow stimulation techniques, or grafting with the use of
allograft or autograft materials. In general, the evidence supporting these surgical
treatment options is lacking, with few comparative and sparse high-level studies, most of
which are level IV studies.20
Indications
Displaced osteochondral fragment
Failed nonsurgical management
Surgical management is primarily based on lesion size.
Smaller than 1.5 cm2: excision and curettage or bone marrow stimulation
This cutoff value is a subject of debate, with consideration of 1-cm2 and 5-mm depths as
more appropriate cutoff values.21
Cartilage cap intact: retrograde drilling and/or bone grafting
Larger than 1.5 cm2 and displaced: open reduction and internal fixation versus
osteochondral or chondral grafting

Indications
Surgical management is indicated in patients in whom a trial of nonsurgical treatment,
generally 3 to 6 months, for the management of an acute displaced fragment fails. In
general, the goals of surgical management are to create a stable cartilage surface and a
more functional joint. The specific procedure depends on the size and location of the
lesion, patient-specific factors, and surgeon preference. Comparative studies to guide
surgical management are lacking.
For smaller lesions, traditionally smaller than 1.5 cm, débridement of the lesion with
consideration of drilling or microfracture is the mainstay of management.22,23

15/28

Lesions larger than 1.5 cm generally are managed via a grafting technique. The approach
selected must consider the size of the lesion, the depth of the lesion, and any bone loss.
Concomitant bone loss is managed via autograft or allograft techniques.
Contraindications
Tibiotalar arthritis
Some consider smoking and poorly controlled diabetes mellitus to be relative
contraindications.
Techniques/Procedures
Débridement and microfracture
Often considered the first-line surgical treatment option
Thought of as the standard treatment option for lesions smaller than 1 to 1.5 cm2
Involves arthroscopic débridement of cartilage to a stable rim and perforating subchondral
bone to encourage healing
Perforations, 3 to 5 mm apart, performed with microfracture awl, Kirschner wire, or small
drill. Some surgeons think that using a drill or a Kirschner wire may cause local bone thermal
necrosis and prefer to use an awl.
Stimulates fibrocartilage formation (type I cartilage)
Better outcomes associated with smaller lesions, contained lesions
Retrograde drilling
Indicated for a bony or cystic lesion with overlying intact cartilage
Integrity of the cartilage cap is confirmed via arthroscopic examination.
Drilling is performed in a retrograde fashion through the talus and into the bony defect to
encourage healing. (Figure 5)
Can be curetted and grafted via this approach if necessary

16/28

Figure 5 Illustrations of the ankle show retrograde drilling, with drill guide placement (A) and
bone grafting (B). (Reproduced from Raikin SM, Mangan JJ: Arthroscopic treatment of
osteochondral lesions of the talus, in Colvin AC, Flatow E, eds: Atlas of Essential Orthopaedic
Procedures, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 695-703.
Autologous chondrocyte implantation (ACI)
Two-stage procedure
Autograft hyaline cartilage is harvested, grown in a laboratory over the course of several
weeks, and replanted into the débrided defect with overlying autologous periosteal
coverage.
May be considered in patients in whom microfracture fails
Successful outcome not associated with lesion size
Bone grafting may be necessary for deeper (>5 mm) lesions.
Matrix-induced ACI
Two-stage procedure
Similar to ACI but uses a matrix to secure the chondrocytes to the defect.

Autologous matrix-induced chondrogenesis
Bone marrow progenitors harvested and replanted during the same procedure
Uses iliac crest bone marrow aspirate concentrate or platelet-rich plasma on a collagen
matrix scaffold to fill prepared defect
Another option is to mix the bone marrow aspirate concentrate with acellular particulated
allograft.
Osteochondral autograft transfer
Used for large lesions, lesions without a stable bony rim, and shoulder lesions
Autograft osteochondral plugs are harvested, generally from the knee or the talus.
The site is débrided and measured, and plugs are placed into the defect.
Donor site morbidity is a disadvantage, and the procedure is technically challenging.
Frequently, a malleolar osteotomy is required to access the joint for graft placement.
Osteochondral allograft
Fresh or fresh-frozen grafts; fresh are superior
Generally used for larger defects with bone loss and shoulder lesions
Can use plugs or a size-matched bulk allograft
Frequently, a malleolar osteotomy is required for graft placement.
Particulated juvenile cartilage allograft trasplantation
Particulated cartilage allograft containing live cells from young donors
Single-stage procedure
Secured to prepared lesion with the use of fibrin glue
Bone grafting may be necessary for deeper (>5 mm) lesions
Limitations include availability of material and cost

Techniques/Procedures
For smaller lesions, traditionally smaller than 1.5 cm, débridement of the lesion with
microfracture is the mainstay of management. The OLT is arthroscopically débrided to a
stable rim, and the subchondral bone is then perforated with the use of a drill or a
microfracture awl. Outcomes have been consistently favorable with the use of a lesion
cutoff value of 1.5 cm,2,22,23 with success rates ranging from 65% to 90% and a success
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:28 PM
AAOS | Osteochondral Lesions of the Talus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000007
18/28

rate of approximately 85% reported in a systematic review.24 A longer term study with 8-
to 20-year follow-up reported 78% excellent or good results.25 Uncontained shoulder
lesions managed via marrow stimulation may result in poorer outcomes.26 Outcomes
seem to be similar in cystic lesions, with several studies, including a recent level II
prospective study, reporting no difference in outcomes for lesions smaller than 1.5 cm2
regardless of the presence of subchondral cyst.27,28 Microfracture with biologic adjuncts
is promising, with randomized trials of platelet-rich plasma reporting improved results
compared with microfracture alone and with hyaluronic acid.29
Retrograde drilling allows for management of the underlying bony pathology without
disruption of an intact cartilage rim. This technique involves arthroscopically examining
the cartilage surface to verify that it is intact, and then drilling through the talus into the
lesion. The cartilage surface is visualized during drilling, and care is taken to not violate
the cartilage rim. The lesion can be curetted and packed with the use of bone graft, if
necessary, through the drill tract. Clinical and second-look arthroscopic outcomes are
favorable with this technique.30
ACI is a two-stage procedure that often is performed after failed microfracture.
Chondrocytes are harvested from the anterior talus or the non–weight-bearing surface
of the knee and cultured for 3 to 8 weeks; they can remain viable for more than 1 year.
They are then replanted during a second procedure and covered with the use of a
periosteal patch, usually from the tibia. Results are positive, with success rates ranging
from 81.2% to 100%, and are not related to lesion size.31
Matrix-induced ACI is similar to ACI, with the benefit of using a matrix for implantation,
which eliminates the periosteal patch necessary for ACI. This allows the procedure to be
performed arthroscopically if lesion size and position allow. A meta-analysis of case
series reported an overall success rate of 89.9% (range, 50% to 100%), with mean lesion
size of 2.3 cm2 and a follow-up of almost 3 years32 (Video 1).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:28 PM
AAOS | Osteochondral Lesions of the Talus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000007
19/28

Autologous matrix-induced chondrogenesis is a single-stage procedure during which
bone marrow progenitor cells are harvested and implanted onto a collagen matrix
scaffold to fill a prepared defect. The procedure can be performed completely
arthroscopically or as an open procedure if necessary to fully access the OLT. Overall
results are promising. One study with a 2- to 8-year follow-up reported considerable
improvements in pain and functional scores; however, MRI findings did not correlate
with functional scores and revealed cartilage hypertrophy in more than one-half of the
patients and bone edema in almost all the patients.33 A recent meta-analysis also found
considerable improvements in pain and functional scores across 492 patients; however,
the authors were unable to correlate such improvements with lesion size or approach.34
In the osteochondral autograft transfer technique, osteochondral plugs are obtained
from the ipsilateral non–weight-bearing knee, calcaneus, or talus. These grafts can
maintain viable hyaline cartilage but may result in donor site morbidity. In general, the
technique is indicated in patients with a large lesion or in patients undergoing revision
and is performed via an open approach. The lesion is measured and, depending on the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:28 PM
AAOS | Osteochondral Lesions of the Talus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000007
20/28

size of the lesion, a single plug or multiple plugs (mosaicplasty) can be used. Outcomes
of the procedure are good, with considerable improvements in pain and functional
scores and good/excellent outcomes reported in 87% of ankles in systematic review of
11 level IV studies.35 Autograft may be superior to allograft with regard to functional and
radiographic findings.36 The rate of donor site morbidity reported in the literature varies;
however, it is a major disadvantage of this procedure.37
Osteochondral allografts are preferably fresh, size-matched talar grafts that are used to
manage large and uncontained shoulder lesions. The benefits of allograft over autograft
are the ability to size-match the defect for better fit and the elimination of donor site
morbidity. Graft can be obtained as a plug or as a bulk allograft, depending on the lesion
characteristics and size. The lesion is measured on preoperative CT scans, and the donor
is size matched. After a fresh, matched specimen is located, it should be implanted
within 3 to 4 weeks. Outcomes of allograft are mixed, with a longer series with a follow-
up of 11 years reporting conversion to ankle fusion in approximately one-third of
patients.38 Fourteen patients followed prospectively experienced considerable
improvements in pain and functional scores, with an overall success rate of 86%;
however, five patients required revision surgery for pain and stiffness.39 Graft
subsidence, nonunion, resorption, and joint space narrowing are frequent
complications.18
Particulated juvenile cartilage allograft transplantation is a method in which allograft
cartilage from juvenile donors is implanted into a prepared lesion. It can be performed
via an open or arthroscopic approach and can be used in primary or revision
procedures. Long-term results in the literature are lacking, and short-term results in the
literature vary. An early study reported 92% good to excellent results and one
delamination at a follow-up of16 months.40 A study comparing particulated juvenile
cartilage allograft transplantation and microfracture with and without bone marrow
aspirate concentrate reported similar functional outcome scores in both groups.41 Some
studies have reported higher failure rates and persistent pain, with lesion size associated
with failure.42,43

Preoperative Planning
Preoperative imaging: radiography, CT, MRI; consider weight-bearing CT in patients with
deformity
Consider managing concomitant pathology: ankle ligament instability, varus hindfoot

Preoperative Planning
A strong preoperative plan is critical in the management of OLTs. Complete preoperative
imaging studies should be performed and analyzed to determine what procedure is
most appropriate. Appropriate preoperative patient discussions and counseling are
essential. Instability or deformity, if present, should be addressed.
Patient Positioning
Patient positioning is based on the approach to the lesion.
For anterior lesions, the patient typically is placed in the supine position. This allows for an
open or arthroscopic approach.
Posterior lesions may require prone positioning with posterior arthroscopy.
Central lesions are based on surgeon preference, with patients generally positioned supine.
Concomitant procedures (such as ligament reconstruction, osteotomies) may affect patient
positioning.
Surgical Approaches
Arthroscopic, open, or hybrid approach can be used.
The results of arthroscopic versus open techniques are comparable.
Osteotomies may be necessary to access central or large lesions.
